assessment.nobel_worthiness: Methods for estimating demand and supply in differentiated-product markets, together with dynamic oligopoly frameworks, made empirical industrial organisation quantitative. They are now the standard tools for merger review, antitrust and welfare analysis, and for much applied work in trade and health. The impact on both research and policy practice is large and clearly traceable.
assessment.attribution: The core demand-estimation contribution is concentrated in the Berry–Levinsohn–Pakes work, with Pakes also central to dynamic industry models. The longlist credits seven names, so the three-person cap excludes real contributors (Bresnahan, Benkard, Reiss, Levin). Choosing the BLP trio is the cleanest attribution.
assessment.maturity: The main contributions date from the 1990s, and decades of application and extension have confirmed their value. Timing is not a concern.
uncertainties: Bresnahan's and Berry's relative claims on the demand-side framework could be weighed differently.
Whether the committee prefers a methods prize in IO this soon after other methods prizes (2021 causal inference).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory changed how economists understand who trades, the gains from trade, and the reallocation effects of liberalisation. It also opened a large empirical agenda using firm-level data, and the framework is now the workhorse of modern trade analysis.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the pivotal theoretical contribution, and Helpman's work with Melitz and Yeaple on exporting versus FDI extended it. Redding is a major contributor to the quantitative follow-on literature but is a less obvious third laureate. Related earlier contributions, such as Bernard–Jensen on empirical facts, are not on this ballot.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of confirmation in theory, structural work and policy evaluation. Trade has not been recognised since 2008, so timing is plausible.
uncertainties: Credit division with empirical precursors on exporter premia.
Helpman also appears under another candidate, so the committee may weigh which of his bodies of work to recognise.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: A rigorous empirical account of how technology and import competition reshaped labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality. The China-shock work showed persistent regional adjustment costs, which has had major policy influence. The research design is credible and transparent in the quasi-experimental tradition.
assessment.attribution: The China-shock contribution is clearly attributable to Autor, Dorn and Hanson. The task-based framework has wider origins (Autor, Levy and Murnane; Acemoglu and Restrepo), and the longlist omits some of those names. Katz, also listed, is better known for the earlier education–technology race work.
assessment.maturity: Roughly fifteen years since the main papers, with extensive replication and extension. There is some continuing debate over magnitudes and mechanisms, but the central findings have held up.
uncertainties: Overlap in theme with recent prizes on technology and institutions.
Debate about the size of the China-shock effects and the generality of its findings.
Whether the task-framework credit should be given to a broader group.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Construction of long-run top-income series from tax data transformed the measurement of inequality and reoriented a whole research agenda and public debate. The data and methodological innovation is lasting, and Saez's work links it to optimal tax policy.
assessment.attribution: Piketty–Saez top-income series are the core, with Zucman's later work on offshore wealth and distributional national accounts as an extension. The two-person selection reflects the foundational data contribution. The case for adding Zucman rests on more recent work.
assessment.maturity: The top-income work is twenty years old. The wealth-tax and wealth-concentration claims are more contested and less settled.
uncertainties: Methodological disputes over wealth-inequality estimates and capital-share arguments.
Whether the committee values the measurement contribution above the more contested theoretical and policy claims.
The role of Atkinson, deceased, and Kuznets-era precursors in credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data used to measure intergenerational mobility and the causal effect of neighbourhoods. The work has changed what is measurable and has had unusually wide policy and academic influence, building on the credibility-revolution tradition.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the leading figure of the program, and Hendren is central to the causal neighbourhood-effects work. Friedman and Katz are significant collaborators (Katz in the Moving to Opportunity reanalysis). The attribution is team-based, which complicates the three-person limit.
assessment.maturity: The central results are about a decade old. Replication and follow-up research is substantial but not fully mature, and some findings (e.g. on neighbourhood effects) are still being extended.
uncertainties: Early in the career arc relative to other candidates.
Whether the contribution is mainly data and measurement rather than a distinct conceptual advance.
Team-based credit within Opportunity Insights.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantified how misallocation of inputs across firms can account for a large share of cross-country income differences. This shaped growth and development economics and spawned a large literature on frictions and productivity measurement.
assessment.attribution: The core is Hsieh–Klenow (2009), with Restuccia–Rogerson as a closely related parallel contribution. Restuccia is on the list but the two-person choice follows the most-cited paper, which makes attribution somewhat arbitrary.
assessment.maturity: Fifteen or more years of application. Measurement challenges, such as markup versus distortion interpretation and measurement error, are acknowledged in the literature.
uncertainties: Sensitivity to measurement error and to the interpretation of dispersion in marginal products.
Overlap with the 2025 prize on growth and with earlier growth prizes.
Omission of Restuccia and Rogerson from the proposed pair.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers bargaining model gave a tractable non-cooperative foundation for bargaining and underpins models of wages, search and market trade. It is a core piece of the modern microeconomic toolkit.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein (1982) is the founding contribution, and Rubinstein–Wolinsky links bargaining to decentralised markets. Binmore's contributions, and Stahl's, are close precursors. Credit for the underlying idea is therefore somewhat diffuse.
assessment.maturity: More than forty years of use, so confirmation is complete. The question is whether the committee still sees it as the field's most pressing recognition gap.
uncertainties: Relative priority among theory-only candidates.
Precursor credit to Stahl and Binmore.
Possible view that game theory has recently been recognised several times.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidity micro-foundations and the New Keynesian framework underpin most modern monetary policy analysis and central-bank modelling. The influence on policy practice is large.
assessment.attribution: Attribution is the main difficulty. Calvo pricing, Taylor's staggered contracts and policy rule, and Woodford's synthesis are central, but Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and others are also important. Any three-person selection will leave out major contributors.
assessment.maturity: The foundations date back 30 to 45 years, and the framework has been extensively tested. Recent inflation episodes have prompted debate about model adequacy.
uncertainties: Eight names are credited, so three-person attribution is contestable.
Overlap with earlier macroeconomics prizes.
Doubts about the framework's empirical fit after the post-2021 inflation.
